name: Lead Research for Action (charityevals)
beneficiaries_note: Our build: the one study whose findings are counted is Malawi's, so the children and adults protected are in Malawi.
summary: Lead Research for Action tests everyday products sold in markets in low- and middle-income countries for lead, so that governments and others know which sources to act on; its first finished study, in Malawi in 2025, found lead in metal cookware, plastic foodware, a hair dye and soils some women eat in pregnancy. We count its spending from October 2024 to October 2026 against that study's expected value: the chance that Malawi acts on its findings, times the blood lead children would lose, valued as later earnings, with adults' heart-disease deaths as a side effect. At the defaults it comes to about {{result}} years of healthy life per $1,000. No action has followed yet, the charity publishes no accounts and nobody has measured how much blood lead these products cause, so the result is mostly uncertainty and is discounted for missing data.

source.title: LEEP, Announcing LEEP's Opportunity Fund Grantees (14 August 2026)
source.quote: This research project will conduct a systematic, market-based study to identify major sources of lead exposure in a high-burden country where data is currently lacking.
source.note: The grant's amount is not published.

rows.explainer: The charity publishes no accounts: its US money runs through a fiscal sponsor (Players Philanthropy Fund) whose return doesn't split its projects, and its UK charity (no. 1218900) was registered in July 2026, its first return not yet due. The seed grant covered about its first year with two co-founders; by 2026 the team page lists five staff, and it won a further grant from LEEP's Opportunity Fund in August 2026 for a study in another country. With lab testing in the US, a field partner in Malawi and travel, our judgment is about $600,000 over the two years ($400,000 to $900,000), in about 2025 prices: about $336,000 beyond the seed grant ($136,000 to $636,000).

rows.label: Births a year, Malawi (2023)
rows.explainer: The shared figure (facts: malawi, UN World Population Prospects). If Malawi acts on the findings, each year's newborns grow up with less lead: the children a year of protection reaches.

rows.label: Children a year protected if Malawi acts on the findings
rows.explainer: Each year's births in Malawi.

rows.label: Children's average blood lead in low- and middle-income countries (µg/dL)
rows.explainer: The shared figure (facts: lead), from Ericson et al.'s review of blood lead in low- and middle-income countries.

rows.label: Blood lead a typical Malawian child gets from lead-contaminated metal cookware (µg/dL)

source.title: Lead Research for Action (January 2026), Assessing Lead Exposure Risks from Commonly Used Consumer Products in Malawi (working paper)
source.quote: given that the median Pb concentration for metallic cookware sampled in Malawi was 166 ppm, this suggests that most pots and pans may be below a level of significant concern for this category

rows.explainer: Over half of the 98 pots and pans tested were above 100 ppm, but the median was 166 ppm, which the report itself judges mostly below concern; the distribution is heavily skewed, with some imported non-stick pans over 300,000 ppm (formally made cookware, the most contaminated, is less popular than artisans' pots). Leaching tests of contaminated pots from other low- and middle-income countries (Weidenhamer et al. 2017, Binkhorst et al. 2025, cited in the report) could add over 5 µg/dL to a user, under harsher conditions than everyday cooking. Averaged over all children: a minority of households cooking in badly contaminated pots, at a fraction of the laboratory leaching. Our judgment, 0.4 µg/dL (0.1 to 1.5).

rows.label: Blood lead a typical Malawian child gets from lead in plastic foodware (µg/dL)

source.title: Lead Research for Action (January 2026), Assessing Lead Exposure Risks from Commonly Used Consumer Products in Malawi (working paper)
source.quote: LeRA is currently conducting leachability testing to ascertain the lead exposure level associated with use of lead-contaminated plastic foodware

rows.explainer: Every consumer interviewed uses plastic plates and cups, which averaged 442 ppm (median 14 ppm, up to 7,100 ppm), the lead mostly in the pigment of green, orange and red items. Lead bound in plastic leaches far less than lead in metal, and the charity's own leaching tests are not out. Our judgment, 0.1 µg/dL (0.02 to 0.5).

rows.label: Blood lead a typical Malawian child gets from the lead hair dye (µg/dL)

source.title: Lead Research for Action (January 2026), Assessing Lead Exposure Risks from Commonly Used Consumer Products in Malawi (working paper)
source.quote: Other hair dyes sampled in this study were not found to have high Pb concentrations

rows.explainer: One product, a progressive hair dye at 1.4% lead, which the report's model puts at about 0.76 µg/dL in a user's child through hand-to-mouth contact; the other hair dyes tested were low. If a few percent of households use it: our judgment, 0.02 µg/dL averaged over all children (0.005 to 0.1).

rows.label: Share of children's blood lead from the products the study flagged for limits (metal cookware, plastic foodware, a lead hair dye)
rows.explainer: The three products' blood lead below, summed, over a typical child's blood lead: a share used for adults' deaths too.

rows.label: IQ points lost per µg/dL of blood lead in childhood
rows.explainer: The shared figure (facts: lead), from the seven-cohort pooled analysis of Lanphear et al. (2005).

rows.label: IQ points a child keeps if the flagged products are made lead-free
rows.explainer: Children's blood lead × the flagged products' share of it × the IQ loss per µg/dL: the three products' blood lead × the loss per µg/dL.

rows.label: Increase in earnings per IQ point
rows.explainer: The shared figure (GiveWell, {{row:iq_wage_gain}} per IQ point), read as a gain in ln(consumption).

rows.label: Household sharing multiplier on an earnings gain
rows.explainer: The shared figure (GiveWell): an earner's gain is shared with the household.

rows.label: Years an IQ gain raises earnings, discounted
rows.explainer: The shared working life of 40 years (facts: givewell_shared.long_term_benefit_years), discounted at the shared rate.

rows.label: Average years a year's sales of the flagged products keep exposing children
rows.explainer: A pot or plate sold this year exposes its household for as long as it is used. Plastic plates and cups last a year or two and a hair dye months; aluminium pots are used for many years and handed down. Weighted towards the pots, which carry most of the lead below. Our judgment, 5 years (2 to 12).

rows.label: Years from a child's exposure to working age
rows.explainer: The shared figure (facts: lead): lead harms the brain most before about age six, and earnings start at about 20.

rows.label: Discount for the products' exposure coming over their life
rows.explainer: The exposure a year's averted source would have caused fades at a constant rate over its life; discounted continuously at the shared rate, its present value is (1/life) ÷ (1/life + ln(1 + rate)) of the undiscounted whole.

rows.label: Discount for the waits until the earnings gain begins
rows.explainer: The exposure's spread over its life, then the years until the exposed children reach working age, at the shared rate.

rows.label: Birth cohorts' worth of exposure averted per year the flagged products are kept lead-free
rows.explainer: Each year's sales cause that year's share of the harm for as long as the products last: summed over their life, about one birth cohort's childhood of exposure from them. A growing market puts more in each year's sales, and products that are thrown away early put less. Our judgment, 1 (0.5 to 1.6).

rows.label: Earnings value per child born in the country per year of protection, in units of value
rows.formula: iq_points_per_child * iq_wage_gain * resource_sharing * iq_years * income_wait_discount * $uov_per_ln_consumption * cohorts_per_win_year
rows.explainer: IQ points kept × earnings per point × household sharing × discounted working years, after the waits, on the shared ln(consumption) scale, per cohort's worth of exposure averted.

rows.label: Deaths attributed to lead exposure worldwide, 2023
rows.explainer: The shared figure (facts: lead, from WHO and IHME's Global Burden of Disease Study 2023): lead's deaths from all sources, mostly adults' heart disease from a lifetime's exposure.

rows.label: Births worldwide, 2023
rows.explainer: The shared figure (facts: lead, UN World Population Prospects): to express lead's deaths per child born, the unit this model counts.

rows.label: People aged 65 or older, Malawi (2023)
rows.explainer: The shared figure (facts: malawi, UN World Population Prospects). Lead's deaths are mostly heart disease at older ages, so how many older adults Malawi has per child born sets how many lead deaths a cut in its blood lead can avert.

rows.label: People aged 65 or older, world (2023)
rows.explainer: The shared figure (facts: lead, UN World Population Prospects): the same for the world, whose lead deaths per birth the row below starts from.

rows.label: Malawi's older adults per birth, relative to the world's
rows.explainer: Malawi's population is younger than the world's, so a year of lower blood lead there averts fewer of the heart-disease deaths that make up most of lead's death toll. Its people aged 65 or older per birth over the world's: a proxy for the ages at which lead's deaths come (50 and over); blood lead in adults is taken as the same as the world's.

rows.label: The flagged products' share of adults' blood lead, relative to their share of children's
rows.explainer: Pots and foodware put lead into the whole household's food, so adults eat it too; young children absorb more of the lead they swallow (up to four to five times as much as adults, by WHO's fact sheet on lead) but eat less, and they are the hair dye's main victims through hand-to-mouth contact; adults' blood lead also comes from work and lead stored in bone. Our judgment, 80% (40% to 120%).

rows.label: Value of a heart-disease death averted, at the world's ages (units of value)
rows.explainer: The ages of the world's cardiovascular deaths (facts: death_ages) valued by GiveWell's weights by age, the 70-and-over band split by the share at 80 or older, × the value-of-a-life slider: lead's deaths are mostly heart disease in older adults. The shared facts hold the world's age split only (and the UK's and US's); a younger country's heart-disease deaths come somewhat younger, so this slightly undervalues each death.

rows.label: Side effect: adults' lead deaths averted, value per child born per year of protection (units of value)
rows.formula: lead_deaths_2023 / world_births_2023 * age_structure_adj * source_share * adult_vs_child_exposure * lead_cvd_value_per_death * exposure_pv * cohorts_per_win_year
rows.explainer: Lead in food raises adults' blood pressure and heart disease. Lead's deaths per birth worldwide, scaled to Malawi's younger population, × the flagged products' share of adults' blood lead (their share of children's × the adult ratio), valued at the shared value of a death by age, over the products' life. Illness short of death and kidney disease aren't counted: lead's burden is mostly deaths.

rows.label: Value per child born in Malawi per year of protection, in units of value
rows.explainer: Children's later earnings and adults' deaths averted, per child born per year the source is kept down.

rows.label: Malawi's record on acting on lead findings, relative to a typical contested policy issue

source.title: Lead Research for Action (March 2026), Lead Exposure Risks from Consumer Products in Malawi: Key Recommendations and Next Steps
source.quote: LeRA recommends use of the European Union’s maximum allowable level of lead in plastic packaging of 100 ppm as an interim regulatory limit.

rows.explainer: For: the limits it recommends are ready-made (the EU's 100 ppm for plastics, the UN Food and Agriculture Organization's 100 ppm for metal cans as a reference for cookware), lead-free plastics are widely available, and Malawi's Bureau of Standards has enforced a lead limit before (paint, which the study left out for that reason). Against: no meeting with a ministry or the Bureau, and no draft limit, is reported in the ten months since the report; the charity's next steps include more research before rules; it does not campaign itself; and the informal cookware made by artisans from scrap is hard to regulate. Our judgment, 0.4 (0.15 to 1) times the base rate.

rows.label: Chance that Malawi limits lead in a flagged product (the products branch)
rows.explainer: One event: Malawi sets and enforces a lead limit for at least one of the flagged products (plastic foodware, cookware, imported non-stick pans, lead hair dye); which products a limit covers is the implementation rows. The shared chance that a contested policy issue changes within about four years (@democracy.lobbied_issue_change_rate), times Malawi's own record above. The soils branch has its own chance.

rows.label: Years a won reform counts before it would have come anyway
rows.explainer: The site's one answer (Your values → How impact is counted; docs/normalization.md 2.9). Never the charity's or an evaluator's own years.

rows.label: Years from the middle of the period's spending until a limit applies
rows.explainer: Counted from October 2025, the middle of the spending it is charged to. The charity plans leachability results and further testing first; a national standard then needs drafting, adoption and a transition for makers and importers, so the earliest a limit applies is about 2028. Our judgment, 5 years (3 to 9); how much of the market a limit clears is the implementation rows.

rows.label: Discount for the wait until a limit applies
rows.explainer: The wait discounted at the shared rate, like every future benefit.

rows.label: Discounted years of impact of a limit
rows.explainer: The years a won reform counts, discounted, after the wait until the limit applies.

rows.label: Flagged products: expected value of Malawi limiting them (before adjustments)
rows.explainer: Children a year × value per child × the chance of action × the discounted years.

rows.label: Soils eaten in pregnancy: share of pregnancies in which the mother eats them

source.title: Lead Research for Action (January 2026), Assessing Lead Exposure Risks from Commonly Used Consumer Products in Malawi (working paper)
source.quote: 50% of the women who had consumed soils in the past ate them regularly while pregnant

rows.explainer: 26% of the women interviewed said they had eaten the soils sold for pregnancy cravings, now or in the past, and half of those ate them regularly while pregnant: about 13% of pregnancies. The report suspects under-reporting from social desirability. 15% (8% to 30%).

rows.label: Soils eaten in pregnancy: rise in the foetus's blood lead over the pregnancy (µg/dL)

source.title: Lead Research for Action (January 2026), Assessing Lead Exposure Risks from Commonly Used Consumer Products in Malawi (working paper)
source.quote: this would suggest an average foetal BLL over the duration of the pregnancy in the range of 3.65-4.69ug/dL

rows.explainer: The report's biokinetic model: 16 g a day at 48 ppm for the first three months raises the mother's blood lead by 5.21 µg/dL on average over the pregnancy, the foetus's by 3.65 to 4.69. The recommendations report calls these highly uncertain (the lead's bioavailability in the soils is unknown; no blood was tested), so the range is widened below: 4.2 µg/dL (1.5 to 5.5).

rows.label: Soils eaten in pregnancy: weight of a pregnancy's blood lead against a childhood's
rows.explainer: The IQ loss per µg/dL is measured against children's blood lead averaged over the early years, about six of them; a pregnancy's raised blood lead lasts about nine months, an eighth of that span. The developing brain is more sensitive before birth, which raises it. Our judgment, 15% (6% to 35%).

rows.label: Soils eaten in pregnancy: IQ points per child born if the practice stopped
rows.explainer: Share of pregnancies exposed × the foetus's blood-lead rise × its weight against a childhood × the IQ loss per µg/dL, averaged over all births.

rows.label: Soils eaten in pregnancy: years from the exposure to working age
rows.explainer: The exposure comes before birth and earnings start at about 20. Our judgment, 20 years (18 to 22).

rows.label: Soils eaten in pregnancy: earnings value per child born per year of an intervention, in units of value
rows.explainer: The same earnings chain as the products'; each year of an intervention reaches that year's pregnancies, one birth cohort.

rows.label: Soils eaten in pregnancy: the chance of an intervention, relative to a typical contested policy issue

source.title: Lead Research for Action (March 2026), Lead Exposure Risks from Consumer Products in Malawi: Key Recommendations and Next Steps
source.page: p. 6, Summary of Recommended Next Steps
source.quote: LeRA believes that the key next step on geophagic pregnancy soils is to quantify the blood lead level effect of consuming soils during pregnancy.

rows.explainer: Its own next step is a blood-lead study; only if that finds a large effect does it recommend an intervention (awareness campaigns or nutritional supplements), which a health ministry or NGO would have to fund and run against a long-standing cultural practice. Our judgment, 0.3 (0.1 to 0.8) times the base rate.

rows.label: Soils eaten in pregnancy: chance that Malawi runs an intervention
rows.explainer: One event: a health ministry or NGO programme against eating lead-contaminated soils in pregnancy. The shared base rate (@democracy.lobbied_issue_change_rate) times the record above.

rows.label: Soils eaten in pregnancy: expected value (before adjustments)
rows.explainer: Children a year × value per child × the chance of an intervention × the discounted years, with the same wait as the products' limits.

rows.label: Expected value of the Malawi study's findings (before adjustments)
rows.explainer: The two branches summed, for reading; each takes its own delivery and work-done shares in the outcome.

rows.label: Money moved or raised for other charities in the period (US$)

source.title: Lead Research for Action, Assessing Lead Exposure Risks from Commonly Used Consumer Products in Malawi (blog, 9 February 2026)
source.quote: LeRA sampled 747 consumer products from 24 markets across three Malawian districts, spanning 12 product categories.

rows.explainer: None: the charity runs its own studies and moves no money to other charities.

rows.label: Value of a dollar where shifted money would otherwise have gone (our judgment: 1× GiveDirectly), units of value
rows.explainer: Our judgment. Shifted money was going to be given anyway; it is credited only for the gain. Where it would have gone is valued at GiveDirectly's live result (GiveWell's model), as Ambitious Impact does, times a shared multiple (1×, from 0 to 3×).

rows.label: Share of money moved that is new money
rows.explainer: The site's one figure for every meta charity: about half the money moved wouldn't otherwise have been given (Ambitious Impact's Effective Giving Incubation report), from 35% to 80%.

rows.label: This charity's share of the good done with money, work or budgets it brings in
rows.explainer: The site's one setting for resources another party commits only because of the organisation (docs/normalization.md 2.24): the charity is credited this share of the good done with them, net of their cost; the rest stays with those who paid or did the work.

rows.explainer: New money counts in full; shifted money counts for the gain over where it would have gone. The donors gave it, so the organisation is credited its share of that good (mobiliser_share).

rows.explainer: The site's shared default (facts/meta.json); no careers are changed, so it adds nothing.

rows.label: Value of one career change (units of value)
rows.explainer: The site's one career-change step (docs/normalization.md 2.8), at the mobiliser's share (2.24): the person gives up the pay.

rows.label: Value of the career changes (units of value)
Evidence adjustment: how far the lead-to-IQ-to-earnings and lead-to-heart-disease links should be trusted here
rows.explainer: The IQ loss per µg/dL comes from cohort studies that adjust for confounders but can't remove all of them (the slope is backed by the IQ gains after leaded petrol was phased out); the cohorts are from rich countries, Mexico and Yugoslavia. The IQ-to-earnings link is GiveWell's shared figure. Adults' deaths rest on the Global Burden of Disease study's blood lead to blood pressure to heart disease link, which the same caution fits. How much blood lead the products cause has its own rows. Our judgment, 0.7 (0.4 to 1.0), for both.

rows.label: Share of the outcome that wouldn't have happened anyway
rows.explainer: 1: the years a won reform counts already take in that someone would have found and acted on these sources some day (templates.md Convention 5); no one else was testing consumer products in Malawi's markets.

rows.label: The charity's share of the research and campaigning behind an action
rows.explainer: The charity found the sources and wrote the recommendations (its Malawi field partner, the Lakeland Foundation, was part of the study it paid for). An action would also need others to press for it and design it: the charity names Malawi's government and NGOs, and LEEP runs the plastics leachability tests with it. The ministries and Bureau of Standards that set and enforce a limit, the makers who reformulate and whoever runs a health programme are the adopters: their part is under the mobiliser's share, not this one (docs/normalization.md 2.24). Our judgment, 40% (20% to 70%), for both branches.

rows.label: Share of credit used
rows.explainer: The share among co-researchers and campaigners times the mobiliser's share: the rest of the credit stays with those who carry out the result (docs/normalization.md 2.24).

rows.label: Flagged products: share of their lead exposure under the limits Malawi adopts, if it acts

source.title: Lead Research for Action (March 2026), Lead Exposure Risks from Consumer Products in Malawi: Key Recommendations and Next Steps
source.quote: Plastic foodware appears to be among the most tractable sources of lead exposure identified in the present study

rows.explainer: The recommendations rank plastic foodware and imported non-stick pans as the easiest to regulate (lead-free alternatives exist; imports can be checked at the border), and the hair dye's lead compound is banned elsewhere; artisans' pots cast from scrap need work with the makers before a rule can bite. A first limit is likely to cover the easy products and the branded pots, not the artisans' ones. Our judgment, 60% of the products' exposure (30% to 90%).

rows.label: Flagged products: share of the covered products' lead removed under the limits

source.title: Forsyth JE et al. (2023), Food safety policy enforcement and associated actions reduce lead chromate adulteration in turmeric across Bangladesh, Environmental Research 232: 116328 (abstract, Europe PMC)
source.quote: The proportion of market turmeric samples containing detectable lead decreased from 47% pre-intervention in 2019 to 0% in 2021

rows.explainer: A limit removes lead only as far as it is enforced. The clearest measured case of a market source removed after a study: in Bangladesh, with news coverage, rapid testing and the food safety authority's penalties, turmeric with detectable lead fell from 47% of market samples to none within two years, the high end. Malawi's markets are informal and its Bureau of Standards small, the low end. Pots already in kitchens are in the products' life above, not here. No impact analysis gives makers' costs of switching, so none is counted; lead-free plastics are widely available. Our judgment, half (20% to 90%).

rows.label: Flagged products: share of their lead exposure a limit removes
rows.explainer: The products a limit covers × how much of their lead it removes.

rows.label: Soils eaten in pregnancy: share of the soils' lead exposure an intervention removes

source.title: Lead Research for Action (January 2026), Assessing Lead Exposure Risks from Commonly Used Consumer Products in Malawi (working paper)
source.quote: iron therapy result in an 8-11 percentage point decrease in prevalence of geophagia in a cohort of Malawian women
source.note: Larson LM et al. (2025), Effects of Ferric Carboxymaltose on Pica among Pregnant Women in Malawi: A Substudy to a Randomized Controlled Trial, The Journal of Nutrition 155(7): 2398-2405, https://doi.org/10.1016/j.tjnut.2025.05.010

rows.explainer: The one trial: in Malawian pregnant women, iron therapy cut the share eating soil by 8 to 11 percentage points (Larson et al. 2025, cited in the report), a large part of those who ate it; an awareness campaign has no trial. A programme reaches only some pregnant women, and the soils are sold openly in markets. Our judgment, a quarter of the soils' lead exposure removed (5% to 50%).

rows.label: Soils eaten in pregnancy: share of the charity's own work towards an intervention done by October 2026
rows.explainer: Its own part: finding the soils and their lead (done) and the blood-lead study (under way, more costly). The design and running of an intervention would be others' work, which is in the credit share. Our judgment, 40% (25% to 60%).

rows.label: Counted less where the outcome isn't measured for this charity
rows.explainer: The shared missing-data step (docs/normalization.md 2.12): no action has followed the study yet, and no blood lead is measured; the products' and soils' blood lead, the chances of action and their effects are judgments. Both branches take it.

rows.label: All adjustments shared by the branches combined
rows.explainer: The product of the adjustments that apply to both branches; each branch's delivery and work-done shares apply in the outcome.

rows.label: Side effect: use of the findings beyond Malawi, as a share of the modelled value

source.title: Lead Research for Action (January 2026), Assessing Lead Exposure Risks from Commonly Used Consumer Products in Malawi (working paper)
source.quote: The product was manufactured in Zimbabwe, and was also found by LeRA to be sold in several markets in Kenya, as well as online

rows.explainer: The data are public: the lead hair dye is made in Zimbabwe and sold in Kenya and online, the cookware and plastics results feed other organisations' work on those products, and the methods carry to the next countries. None of it is counted in the chain. Our judgment, a seventh more (none to a half more).

rows.label: Flagged products: share of the charity's own work towards a limit done by October 2026
rows.explainer: The charity's own part only: the study and the recommendations are done; the plastics leachability tests (with LEEP) and its support to the government and partners are still to come. Others' campaigning is in the credit share, not here. Only the share done is charged to the period's spending, so the rest of the value goes with the next dollar. Our judgment, 65% (45% to 85%).

rows.explainer: Each branch with its delivery and work-done shares, the shared adjustments and the side effect; the charity moves no money and changes no careers.
